working_title: The Palace CCTV Ghost That Was Never Explained
alt_title: Hampton Court, 2003: Fire Doors Fly Open, Then a Robed Figure Shuts Them
subject: Hampton Court Palace, October 2003. Fire-door alarms near Clock Court kept going off. CCTV showed the doors flying open, then a grainy robed figure closing them. Historic Royal Palaces' own pages say there is no explanation; the press nicknamed it 'Skeletor'. Accounts differ on how many nights it happened, and a separate 2015 incident was suspected trickery.
why_potential: A real security-camera artefact on a famous royal palace, with the palace's own 'no explanation' statement. Perfect 'one wrong detail' frame (CCTV timestamp + figure). Caught-on-camera is a proven demand format (Top5s, Chills).

references.title: GHOST VIDEOS So Real Even a Cop Can't Debunk Them
references.creator: Slapped Ham

hook_15s: 0-2 s: CCTV-style grey frame, timestamp ticking, fire doors burst open on an empty corridor. VO: 'October 2003. These palace fire doors opened by themselves on camera.' 2-6 s: card 'HAMPTON COURT PALACE'. 6-15 s: 'Security ran to close them. Then the camera caught someone else doing it, someone in a long robe.'
structure: Cold open: CCTV doors burst open
Anchor: Hampton Court, new exhibition, Oct 2003
Stakes: alarms, guards find no one
Witness/artefact: robed figure closes the doors (recreated, not real footage)
Escalation: worldwide headlines; the 'Skeletor' nickname
Skeptic beat: grainy CCTV, a staff prank never ruled out, accounts vary; a 2015 case was suspected trickery
Dead-air reveal: frame-by-frame zoom, the figure's sleeve is the wrong era
Loop: the doors burst open again
thumbnail_concept: CCTV frame with timestamp, open double doors, a pale robed figure half in shadow; text 'NO EXPLANATION'.
animation_style: 3D corridor rendered through a CCTV post-process (low frame rate, noise, timestamp overlay); recreation of the footage only.
scenes: Clock Court corridor with fire doors (CCTV angle)

DOCUMENTED FACT: October 2003 alarms and CCTV of the doors opening, then a robed figure closing them (Historic Royal Palaces; NBC/UPI Dec 2003) [checked 2026-11-27]
The palace states there is no explanation [checked 2026-11-27]
EYEWITNESS CLAIM: Guards found no one; a tourist reported seeing a figure nearby
FOLKLORE: Identification with Tudor-era ghosts; other Hampton Court legends (Catherine Howard)
DRAMATISATION: All CCTV shots are 3D recreations; the real footage is not used; sleeve-detail reveal

working_title: The House Built on a Gallows Site
alt_title: San Diego's Whaley House and the Footsteps of 'Yankee Jim'
subject: Whaley House, Old Town San Diego, built by Thomas Whaley c.1857 (some say 1855/56) on ground where James 'Yankee Jim' Robinson was hanged in 1852 (marker date 18 Sept 1852, for grand larceny). Whaley reportedly attributed heavy footsteps upstairs to Robinson. The house also served as a store, courthouse and theatre, and is now a county-owned museum.
why_potential: Documented gallows history plus a builder who himself reported footsteps; a well-known US haunt (often called one of the most haunted houses in America). Interior is easy to model.

Anchor: Whaley builds in Old Town

Escalation: house becomes courthouse; later museum ghost reports
Skeptic beat: details of the hanging are embellished by ghost tours; dates disputed
Dead-air reveal: the upstairs floorboards dip under an unseen weight
Loop: stairs again

animation_style: Procedural 1850s brick house, oil-lamp lighting, dust; silhouette figures, no execution depicted (rope/beam only as an outline in the flashback).

DOCUMENTED FACT: Robinson hanged in 1852 (historical marker: 18 Sept 1852, grand larceny); Whaley House built c.1857 on that ground; used as store/courthouse/theatre; now a museum [checked 2026-11-27]
EYEWITNESS CLAIM: Thomas Whaley's reported footsteps (an 1860 journal reference, per secondary sources); visitor reports
DRAMATISATION: Floorboard reveal; the execution is not shown

alt_title: The Edinburgh Vaults Experiment: Did They Know Which Rooms Were Haunted?
subject: Edinburgh's South Bridge Vaults. Psychologist Richard Wiseman and colleagues ran field studies there and at Hampton Court (published in the British Journal of Psychology, 2003). Press reports say 51% of volunteers reported unusual experiences in the vaults labelled 'haunted' vs 35% in 'ghost-free' ones. The paper concluded that environmental factors (draughts, lighting, magnetic variance, expectation) can explain many experiences.
why_potential: A real experiment with numbers is a fresh, credible angle that rides the 2026 skeptic trend. Underground vaults are a strong, cheap visual.

references.title: GHOST VIDEOS So Real Even a Cop Can't Debunk Them

hook_15s: 0-2 s: candle in a stone vault, flame bends sideways. VO: 'Scientists sent hundreds of people into these vaults.' 2-6 s: card 'EDINBURGH, SOUTH BRIDGE VAULTS'. 6-15 s: 'Some rooms were called haunted, others ghost-free. The volunteers weren't told which was which. So what happened?'
structure: Cold open: candle flame bends
Anchor: vault history, a reputation for hauntings
Stakes: the experiment design
Result: 51% vs 35% reported experiences (reported)
Twist: the 'haunted' rooms were darker, colder and bigger
Skeptic/believer balance: Wiseman called parts of the result a mystery
Dead-air reveal: a draught explains the flame, then a second flame bends the other way
Loop: candle again
thumbnail_concept: Brick-vaulted tunnel, a lone volunteer silhouette with a clipboard, a red 'HAUNTED' tag on one archway; text '51%'.
animation_style: Procedural brick vaults, candle and torch volumetrics, data-viz bar overlay (51 vs 35).

DOCUMENTED FACT: Wiseman et al. (2003, British Journal of Psychology) studied Hampton Court and the South Bridge Vaults; experiences correlated with environmental factors [checked 2026-11-27]
51% vs 35% figures from press coverage of the vaults study (ABC News); the year (likely 2001) is not confirmed
FOLKLORE: Individual vault ghost stories told on tours

alt_title: 'Scratching Fanny': The Ghost That Ended in the Pillory
subject: The Cock Lane ghost, London, 1762. Knocking and scratching sounds centred on young Elizabeth Parsons were said to be the spirit of Fanny Lynes accusing William Kent of poisoning her. A committee including Samuel Johnson held séances (Johnson's account of 1 Feb 1762 was published in The Gentleman's Magazine). When the girl was controlled the sounds stopped; she was reportedly caught with a sounding board. Her father Richard Parsons was convicted and pilloried.
why_potential: A famous writer as ghost-buster, a false murder accusation driven by a 'ghost', and a clear twist. Differentiated debunk content.

working_title: The Village With a Ghost for Every Lane
alt_title: Pluckley: How a Kent Village Became 'England's Most Haunted'
subject: Pluckley, Kent. First called 'the most haunted village in England' by Frederick Sanders in the Kentish Express (1950). The 1989 Guinness Book of Records described it that way with 12 ghosts; Guinness later 'rested' the category. A 2025 University of the West of England study traced how the legends grew. Ghost counts range from 10 to 17.
why_potential: A countdown structure across one village (lanes, church, pub, woods) with an honest 'how a legend is manufactured' twist. Weaker scares.
